To fill in the above gaps, we have proposed a crowdsourced virtual reality (CVR) experimental approach, which comprises a process model and a digital platform named Crowdsourced Virtual-reality Research (CrowdVR), as detailed in Part I of this set of companion papers [11] . This Part II focuses on implementing and vali - dating the CVR experimental approach, and demonstrating the unique advantages of the CVR experimental approach when applied to the PED research. In the field of PED research, a widely recognized hierarchical structure categorizes pedestrian behavior into strategic, tactical and operational layers [12] . The strategic-tactical-operational (STO) struc - ture has served as an umbrella concept for pedestrians ’ decisions during navigation for at least two decades. Following this structure, two classic experiments in the PED area, namely bottleneck and exit choice exper - iments, are selected to validate the CVR experimental approach. The two experiments, designed under the guidance of the process model and conducted using CrowdVR [11] , are expected to reproduce consistent results, at strategic, tactical, and locomotion layers, to those previously reported in the PED literature. Moreover, new insights into the field of PED, benefiting from the unique and granular behavioral data produced by the CVR experiments, are expected to be revealed and discussed. These experimental results are expected to demonstrate the feasibility, validity, and advantages of the CVR experimental approach for con - ducting empirical PED research. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 pro - vides a brief introduction of the hierarchical STO structure of pedestrian behavior and the CVR experimental approach. Sections 3 and 4 detail the design, implementation, and results and the bottleneck and exit choice experiments, respectively. Section 5 discusses the advantages and values of the CVR experimental approach for PED research. Lastly, Section 6 concludes the paper. 2. Related work 2.1. Strategic-tactical-operational structure for pedestrian behavior In the field of PED research, pedestrian behavior can be described from three layers based on the widely recognized STO structure [12] . At the bottom layer, the operational behavior refers to local walking de - cisions and physical locomotion executed during route planning. Design rules and control logic flow Specific design criteria must be adhered to ensure the effectiveness of the IDES. The following design rules are established: (1) Sensors must, at a minimum, detect smoke; optimally, they should combine capabilities to monitor real-time temperature and smoke levels. (2) At least one sensor should be positioned between two adjacent dynamic exit signs along the evacuation routes. (3) At least one sensor, the Exit Sensor ( s E ), must be installed near each exit door within its coverage. Its activation inhibits the egress route within its coverage. (4) If a dynamic exit sign cannot direct traffic toward a safe exit via the designated evacuation route, it must display a dissuasive pattern (P d ) in that direction. (5) A dynamic exit sign activates the reversion mechanism when all its associated Pattern Evaluators (PEs) indicate dissuasive pat - terns (P d ). (6) A dynamic exit sign activates the reversion mechanism when it is covered by any activated sensor. evidenceSnippets.resultsDiscussion: Results show the potential of IDES to automatically optimize evacuation procedures and occupant safety during emergencies. Furthermore, the study delves into challenges associated with real-world implementation and offers insights for future applications of this innovative safety solution in more complex built environments. 1. Introduction Increasing urbanization has led to more complex structures like high- rise buildings, large open spaces, underground infrastructures with diverse functions, and rising floorplan areas and population density. Such growing complexity of the built environment significantly in - creases the risk for occupants during emergencies, particularly in fire incidents [ 1 ]. The spread of fire and smoke may quickly block evacua - tion exits, potentially causing stampedes or severe congestion as occu - pants evacuate simultaneously and in a panic way [ 2 ]. Therefore, how to accurately determine safe and effective exit routes is crucial, especially given the complex nature of building egress, vulnerable people who need help, and the potential for rapid hazard escalation [ 3 – 5 ]. Traditional exit signs mark pre-designed exit routes established during the building ’ s design phase, adopted globally as a critical component of building fire services systems [ 6 , 7 ]. These signs have batteries to power emergency lighting and maintain illumination even during power failures. Regarding their placement, emergency exit signs are categorized into two types [ 8 , 9 ]: one type is non-directional signs, positioned above an exit door to indicate the exit ’ s location, and the other type is directional signs, located along evacuation paths to guide movement towards exits. However, traditional exit signs present two significant shortcomings. At the basic function level, their effectiveness is often negligible. Studies have shown that these signs may not be sufficiently visible or intuitive to capture occupants ’ attention during emergencies [ 10 , 11 ]. Without effectively drawing attention and indicating exit locations, the funda - mental purpose of traditional exit signs is not fulfilled. Traditional exit signs fail to provide adaptive guidance at the operational effectiveness level. While these signs indicate pre-determined exit routes, they do not necessarily introduce the safest route in real-time during an evacuation because some doors may not be safe, such as if a fire is nearby [ 12 ]. qa.question: Why VR metro?
qa.answer: VR allows controlled, repeatable, safe manipulation of signage, pressure, audio, and layout. Metro/subway VR studies already show pressure affects spatial knowledge and signage reliance, so the context is methodologically defensible.

qa.question: What are the biggest threats to validity?
qa.answer: Unclear Signature manipulation, EEG movement artifacts, audio overlap with visual epochs, map-specific effects, trial order/familiarity, and interpreting behavior as cognitive load without EEG support. Each has a planned control or sensitivity analysis.

qa.question: What makes this project original?

Introduction More and more people are choosing the subway to travel because of its comfort and punctuality. Especially in a heavy congestion metropolis like Beijing, the subway has become a daily choice of urban mobility, with its share even reaching 47.2 % of the public transportation share in 2019. The subway system is generally in underground space with a much more complicated arrangement than other modes. Therefore, wayfinding in subway stations is very important for subway riders to accomplish their travel activity conveniently. Entering, exiting, trans - ferring and evacuating are all typical wayfinding behaviors in a station. However, wayfinding is a difficult problem, especially in such complex and closed systems as subways. Research on this issue is a recent hot topic of study (Chen et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020). According to previous studies, the factors affecting the efficiency of passenger wayfinding can be summarized as the personal characteristics of passengers (Afrooz et al., 2018), social behaviors (Haghani and Sarvi, 2017), the design of the signage system (Feng et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2021; Shang et al., 2021; Kwee-Meier et al., 2019; Meng and Zhang, 2014)and the complexity of the environment (Feng et al., 2022). In addition, time pressure also has a significant impact on passengers ’ wayfinding behavior in emergency conditions (Zhang et al., 2021; Shang et al., 2021; Kwee-Meier et al., 2019; Meng and Zhang, 2014). Among them, spatial knowledge is considered an important factor in personal characteristics (Andresen et al., 2018), including route knowledge and survey knowledge. The findings emphasize the mediating role of perceived reliability in converting environmental design into behavioral intentions and actions, offering theoretical insights and prac - tical recommendations for optimizing WS design to improve routine services and emergency preparedness in airport management. This impressive statistic reflects not only the escalating role of airports in the global economy and cultural exchange but also underscores the imper - ative for airport management to elevate terminal service standards to ensure seamless passenger journeys. Concurrently, the high passenger throughput also exposes airport terminals to a variety of security threats, emphasizing the critical need for robust public safety measures within these transportation hubs. The Basel-Mulhouse-Freiburg Airport, situ - ated at the French-Swiss border, had to evacuate and close temporarily on the opening day of the 2024 Paris Olympics due to a bomb threat ( “ Basel-Mulhouse airport at French-Swiss border re-opens after bomb alert, ” 2024 ). Kennedy International Airport necessitated an urgent evacuation ( “ JFK Airport escalator fire leads to evacuations in Terminal 8 – NBC New York, ” 2024 ). Introduction Wayfinding is essential for survival, yet individuals demonstrate surprisingly wide variability in this ability.

In our previous studies, we have developed spatial in - terventions in Virtual Reality (VR) to help people integrate spatial representations formed from segmented occluded spaces into one coherent representation.

We found that people with high self-report SOD benefited from such interventions and showed improved spatial memory and wayfinding performance, whereas people with low SOD did not or even showed worse performance, potentially due to the reason that the additional visual information overwhelmed their cognitive systems ( He et al., 2021 ; He, McNamara, & Brown, 2019 ).

evidenceSnippets.methods: Methods 2.1. Participants Ninety-four college participants participated in this experiment for monetary compensation. Participants spent between 90 and 150 min completing the experiment. Ten participants ’ (all females; 4 in the regional-landmark-present condition and 6 in the regional-landmark- absent condition) data were excluded due to unable to finish the experiment because of motion sickness. The final sample comprised 84 participants (43 female), with comparable male-to-female ratios across conditions (experimental: 20:22; control: 21:21). As our study was conducted in a combination of indoor-outdoor virtual environment, we based our sample size on Nazareth et al. ’ s (2019) meta-analysis, which reported a large sex difference ( d = 0.55) in navigation performance across indoor-outdoor virtual environments. Using G*Power 3.1 ( Faul et al., 2007 ), we calculated that 82 participants would be needed to detect a medium-to-large effect size ( f = 0.35) in a three-way ANOVA (Sex, Regional Landmark, SOD) at α = 0.5 and 80 % power. All participants provided written informed consent, and the study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB approval Code: FY23-24-235). All procedures followed institutional guidelines. 2.2. Materials and procedure The general procedure is shown in Fig. 1 . After reading and signing on the consent form, participants completed a demographical survey, self-reported sense of direction scale ( Hegarty et al., 2002 ), three working memory capacity tests ( Draheim et al., 2018 ), two numeracy tests ( Cokely et al., 2012 ; Schwartz et al., 1997 ), and finally a spatial navigation test in VR. 2.2.1. Demographics Participants were asked to report their age, sex and race. 2.2.2. Self-reported sense of direction Participants ’ self-reported navigation ability was measured using the Santa Barbara Sense of Direction (SBSOD) scale ( Hegarty et al., 2002 ). The scale comprises 15 items rated on a 7-point scale, including eight positively worded statements (e.g., "I can usually remember a new route after I have traveled it once") and seven negatively worded statements (e.g., "I don ’ t have a very good ’ mental map ’ of my environment"). evidenceSnippets.resultsDiscussion: results in the literature on sex differences in landmark utilization and decision-making, and highlight the importance of considering the interaction between environmental factors and spatial ability in un - derstanding the sex differences in spatial navigation. Our results also have practical implications for designing navigational aids in complex buildings. 1. Introduction Wayfinding is essential for survival, yet individuals demonstrate surprisingly wide variability in this ability. While numerous factors contribute to such individual differences ( Wolbers & Hegarty, 2010 ), sex differences in landmark utilization — particularly how men and women differentially use global and local landmarks — have received substantial research attention over recent decades ( Astur et al., 1998 , 2004 ; Barkley & Gabriel, 2007 , 2007 ; Dahmani et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2012 ; Nazareth et al., 2019 ). Global landmarks refer to the objects or features that are visible from a distance and provide orientation cues over a larger spatial area, and local landmarks refer to the objects or features within an im - mediate environment that are only visible when in close proximity and provide precise positional information ( Golledge, 1999 ). One important factor contributing to these sex differences may be how men and women utilize global and local landmarks, with men excelling in environments with global landmarks but showing reduced or no sex differences in environments with rich local landmarks ( Astur et al., 1998 , 2004 ; Barkley & Gabriel, 2007 ; C ´ anovas et al., 2011 ). However, a recent sys - tematic review and meta-analysis challenges this theory, suggesting that landmark types do not moderate sex differences ( Nazareth et al., 2019 ). Beyond these mixed findings, existing research has focused exclu - sively on global and local landmarks, overlooking an increasingly prevalent type of navigational aid that we term ’ regional landmarks. ’ This represents a significant theoretical gap, as regional landmarks constitute a fundamentally different category of spatial cue that has been absent from landmark taxonomies in spatial cognition research. These landmarks are commonly found in complex indoor environments such as libraries and hospitals, where different sections are demarcated by distinct wall or floor colors (color zones). evidenceSnippets.methods: Method 2.1. Participants Previous studies on the interaction between wayfinding strategy and navigation aid system ( Fang & Zhou, 2012 ) or the interaction between gender and landmark type ( Lin et al., 2012 ) on wayfinding behaviors reported effect sizes ( η p 2 ) ranging between 0.15 and 0.36, with each group including 15 participants. Given the range of effect sizes and the relatively small sample size per group, a medium effect size f = 0.25 was adopted for the present study. Then, to ensure sufficient statistical power, an estimated power (1- β ) of 0.90 was selected. The sample size was then determined by a priori power analysis using G*Power 3.1 ( Faul et al., 2007 ), focusing on the interaction between 2 wayfinding strategy (a between-subject variable: survey vs. route) and 2 landmark type (a within-subject variable: global vs. local) in a repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) with an alpha level of 0.05, an estimated power of 0.90, and an effect size of 0.25. The analysis determined that a sample size of 46 participants was required. Seven hundred and thirty-seven volunteers with corrected normal vision were recruited from the school community and completed the Chinese version of Spatial Navigation Strategy Scale ( Zhao, 2021 ). Referring to the median split method ( Ulrich et al., 2019 ), the volunteers scoring higher than the median on Orientation Strategy subscale and lower than the median on Route Strategy subscale were taken as in - dividuals with the survey strategy, while those scoring lower than the median on Orientation Strategy subscale and higher than the median on Route Strategy subscale were taken as individuals with the route strat - egy. The volunteers scoring higher or lower than the median on both subscales were excluded. After screening, 46 participants (18 – 27 years old, M age = 21.67, SD = 2.46) with both the survey and route strategies were selected by simple randomization and enrolled in the formal experiment, with 23 participants (12 males, M age = 21.61, SD = 2.41) in the survey strategy group and 23 participants (12 males, M age = 21.74, SD = 2.56) in the route strategy group. evidenceSnippets.resultsDiscussion: results showed that people with survey strategies perceived less stress and performed better when wayfinding with global landmarks than with local landmarks, while those with route strategies showed opposite but insignificant trends. The partial mediating effect of perceived stress revealed that matching survey strategies with global landmarks and route strategies with local landmarks reduced perceived stress, thereby enhancing wayfinding performance. These findings might not only help bridge theoretical gaps in understanding how environmental and personal factors interact to improve wayfinding experience and perfor - mance but also provide practical insights for designing personalized navigation aid systems tailored to in - dividuals ’ wayfinding strategies in real life. 1. Introduction Wayfinding refers to the process of determining the location, iden - tifying and following a route between the start and destination ( Golledge, 1999 ). It takes place in outdoor, urban, indoor, and virtual reality environments ( Wiener et al., 2009 ). Human wayfinding relies predominantly on visual cues, as visual information processing is critical for spatial representation ( Ekstrom, 2015 ). The human brain possesses specialized cellular and brain systems dedicated to encoding visual in - formation during wayfinding, in addition to the location coding system similar to that described in rodents ( Ekstrom, 2015 ). For well-learned spatial environments, primarily visual input might be sufficient to elicit complex representations of spatial environments in humans ( Huffman & Ekstrom, 2019 ). Building on this visual dominance, recognizable features of the environment, such as landmarks, facilitate environmental comprehension, thereby improving wayfinding effi - ciency and experience. Landmarks serve as reference points and assist in wayfinding by providing descriptive cues ( Michon & Denis, 2001 ) and integrating routes ( Jansen-Osmann, 2002 ; Philbeck & O ’ Leary, 2005 ; Tlauka & Wilson, 1994 ). However, the effectiveness and applicability of land - marks appear to depend on an individual ’ s specific wayfinding strategy. People with different wayfinding strategies prefer to use distinct types of spatial knowledge ( G ¨ arling et al., 1981 ; Lawton, 1994 ), which, in turn, can be acquired from information provided by certain types of land - marks ( Hurlebaus et al., 2008 ). For example, Galea and Galparsoro (1994) used a prototype egress model, EXODUS, to investigate evacuation from mass-transport vehicles during fire emergencies. Korhonen et al. (2010) proposed FDS + Evac, an agent-based fire evacuation model, by integrating a Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS) with an evacuation module and accounting for smoke and gas concentrations. FDS + Evac methods have been widely adopted to simulate fire evacuations in different scenarios, such as in tunnels (Kr ´ ol and Kr ´ ol, 2020; Ronchi et al., 2012), subway stations (Lei et al., 2012a; Yang et al., 2013, 2016), and dormitories (Lei et al., 2012b; Lei and Tai, 2019). In empirical studies, frequently observed are instances of self-organised behaviours which are considered as accurate depictions of the collective motion exhibited by pedestrians. evidenceSnippets.resultsDiscussion: results of the real-life experiments, indicating the potential of Minecraft for realistically simulating evacuation processes. To further demonstrate the feasibility of using Minecraft for evacuation studies, we conducted a series of virtual evacuation experiments with different fire configurations and room geometries in Minecraft. The pedestrians were found to keep higher distance towards fire and greater detour angle during the fire emergency in a square room. Furthermore, in the scenario of a fire in a corridor, in addition to the aforementioned fire avoidance behaviours, the pedestrians exhibited orderly queuing and exited the room one by one, resulting in increased walking speeds and thus a faster evacuation for most pedestrians. Finally, one post-experiment survey was designed to assess participants ’ perceptions of the Minecraft environment and the pedestrian behaviours and related psychological factors. The results show that the Minecraft can generate considerate realistic real-life situations, and pedestrians chose self-organised behaviours including away from fire, along the wall and detour towards fire in both survey and evacuation experiments. 1. Introduction Public venues hosting sports events, religious activities and cele - brations tend to attract large crowds. Accidents such as fires in such venues can lead to a substantial number of fatalities and injuries. To reduce casualties, researchers have increasingly investigated pedestrian behaviours during fire emergencies, using mainly either numerical or empirical research methods. In the numerical approach, researchers typically combine evacuation simulation models with fire products to investigate the influence of fire on evacuation processes (Cao et al., 2021). Methodology Virtual reality has been widely adopted as a research tool in the study of evacuation behavior, particularly for examining relative behavioral differences across experimental scenarios.

Prior work has shown that VR enables researchers to systematically manipulate conditions while observing changes in information-seeking, attention allocation, and wayfinding performance ( Dai et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025; Kinateder et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2020; Lovreglio et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2023 ).

Results show that participants in the text-based condition took longer to initiate information-seeking but found signage more quickly once seeking began, indicating distinct behavioral patterns shaped by information modality.

However, limited research has examined how the modality of initial evacuation instructions influences evacuees ’ subsequent interaction with text-based signage.

This research addresses this gap by examining both the effect of initial instruction modality on pre-evacuation information-seeking and the impact of modality consis - tency versus switching on wayfinding performance at decision points.

qa.question: Why do you expect Signature2 to be highest?
qa.answer: Not because “medium information is inherently worse.” The mechanism is that Signature2 may provide enough information to require active interpretation but not enough redundancy to resolve uncertainty quickly. That should increase confirmation cost, scanning, dwell, and EEG load, especially at decision points.

qa.question: What is the role of Audio?
qa.answer: Audio is a controlled condition but also a cognitive/modality factor. Auditory information can alter attention and later processing of visual/text signage; therefore audio_play events need to be modeled or excluded around visual decision epochs.

qa.question: Why VR metro?
qa.answer: VR allows controlled, repeatable, safe manipulation of signage, pressure, audio, and layout. Metro/subway VR studies already show pressure affects spatial knowledge and signage reliance, so the context is methodologically defensible.

qa.question: What are the biggest threats to validity?
qa.answer: Unclear Signature manipulation, EEG movement artifacts, audio overlap with visual epochs, map-specific effects, trial order/familiarity, and interpreting behavior as cognitive load without EEG support. Each has a planned control or sensitivity analysis.

qa.question: What makes this project original?
qa.answer: It combines controlled VR metro signage manipulation, precise Unity/LSL event markers, EEG workload/uncertainty features, and behavior traces to test how signage information design shapes decision uncertainty rather than only evacuation time.

Introduction In high-stress situations, such as disasters, occupants ’ decision- making heavily relies on the initial information available at the moment they become aware of a hazard or an alarm. The effectiveness of this initial information is crucial, as it directly impacts evacuees ’ ability to make quick and informed decisions ( Kinateder et al., 2015; Snopkov ´ a et al., 2022 ). Ensuring that evacuation information is clear and easy to understand is therefore essential for enhancing emergency response and occupant safety ( Kim et al., 2025; Li et al., 2014 ). As built environments become increasingly complex, with multiple exits and variable layouts, reliance on static directional or image-based signage alone may not al - ways suffice ( Zhao et al., 2022 ). While its importance is well recognized, there is a growing concern that the interpretation and interaction with text-based signs are influ - enced by the nature of the initial evacuation information received. qa.question: Why do you expect Signature2 to be highest?
qa.answer: Not because “medium information is inherently worse.” The mechanism is that Signature2 may provide enough information to require active interpretation but not enough redundancy to resolve uncertainty quickly. That should increase confirmation cost, scanning, dwell, and EEG load, especially at decision points.

qa.question: What if Signature2 is not highest?
qa.answer: Then the result still informs signage design. We would test whether load instead tracks information density, decision complexity, audio overlap, or map-specific difficulty. The hypothesis is a planned contrast, not a guaranteed result.

qa.question: Why is sign_readable not enough?
qa.answer: Readable range only means the participant is in a technical condition where the sign could be read. The literature separates perception and compliance; people may see a sign but not follow it, or may fail to attend to the relevant sign despite visibility.

qa.question: How will you prove the Signature manipulation worked?
qa.answer: I will not rely on labels alone. I will build a signature_manipulation_table with information density, arrow count, exit count, redundancy, ambiguity, clarity, continuity, and decision relevance, plus post-trial ratings of clarity/reliability/overload and behavioral errors.

qa.question: Why not just analyze completion time?
qa.answer: Completion time collapses perception, decision, movement, and errors into one outcome. Metro Rescue has markers that allow event-level analysis of sign reading and decision-making; this is more aligned with the mechanism.

qa.question: What makes this project original?
qa.answer: It combines controlled VR metro signage manipulation, precise Unity/LSL event markers, EEG workload/uncertainty features, and behavior traces to test how signage information design shapes decision uncertainty rather than only evacuation time.

evidenceSnippets.methods: methodological constraints. The most impor - tant constraint is participants ’ safety (Vilar et al., 2013). Real-world experiments require participants to interact with real smoke, which puts participants at risk. Another constraint is the difficulty in providing a fully controlled experimental environment (Cao et al., 2019) since a real-world environment always involves nuisance variables such as light and noise. Besides, high cost is also a limitation for researchers to develop a real-world experimental environment (Haghani and Sarvi, 2018). To address these constraints, immersive virtual reality (VR) technology becomes a promising approach. Immersive VR offers a similar degree of ecological validity as classical laboratory studies by providing virtual emergency environments with high quality and immersive experience (Kinateder et al., 2014a). Previous studies also demonstrated that immersive VR could simulate emergencies and evoke participants ’ emotions effectively without putting the participants at risk of physical harm (Kinateder et al., 2014a; Zou et al., 2017; Tucker et al., 2018). Also, immersive VR allows researchers to design experi - mental environments economically and provides high experimental control for human behavior studies (Ronchi et al., 2015; Haghani and Sarvi, 2018). These advantages of immersive VR experiments are in line with the requirements and the scope of this study. Hence, an immersive VR-based controlled experiment was conducted to investigate why people were willing to take a risky shortcut for evacuations even if there was another safe route available. The experiments. In the present experiment, participants ’ risk tolerance was measured using questionnaires, and their route choices were recorded when they evacuated from a virtual building under different smoke scenarios. A high density of smoke reduced the use of a smoky shortcut but did not prevent some participants from using the shortcut...
evidenceSnippets.resultsDiscussion: resulted in 12,025 injuries, 2790 deaths, and a loss of about 10 billion dollars. To respond to indoor fires, people often choose to evacuate from hazardous buildings to a safe place. Hence, evacuation route selection plays a critical role in determining the evacuation efficiency and whether evacuees can leave a hazardous area safely. In a perfect world, people would rationally avoid ongoing or imminent hazards when selecting a route to escape quickly. However, risk-taking behavior is widely observed during evacuations (Lin et al., 2020a). In a building fire, people may be unaware of or underestimate the danger such as smoke and take a risky route for evacuations. Taking a shortcut in a hazardous area such as a smoky corridor or stairs is a typical risk-taking behavior. Moving through smoke has been widely observed in building fire evacuations (Bryan, 1977; Proulx, 2003; Proulx and Fahy, 2008). Proulx et al. (1995) investigated a fire case of a high-rise residential building and found that 95 percent of the responders located above the fire floor tried to use smoky corridors or stairs for evacuations. However, 38.8% of the responders gave up their evacuations and stayed in their units due to too much smoke/heat and left the building finally with the help of firefighters or police officers. Kobes et al. (2010a) conducted a real-world evacuation experiment in a hotel. The results indicated that 31 percent of the participants still used the route blocked by smoke to evacuate even though there were several available evacuation routes without smoke. Hofinger et al. (2014) did an unannounced evacuation drill in a university building and took an after- drill survey of the occupants of the building. The survey indicated that 65 percent of the responders expressed that they would be likely to pass a smoky area for evacuations. Although a shortcut in a smoky area may help individuals evacuate quickly, it is still dangerous. First, it exposes the individuals to hazards directly and increases the risk of injuries or death (Hofinger et al., 2014). Building fires may produce a sub-lethal level of asphyxiant gases such as carbon monoxide. When people are exposed to a high level of carbon monoxide, they would have headaches, difficulty breathing, and other physiological changes (Raub, 2004). Second, the corridors or exits with slight smoke may worsen at any time due to a dynamic fire; hence, a shortcut with slight risk may become a hazardous route. Third, smoke * Corresponding author. Full length article Why individuals do not use emergency exit doors during evacuations: A virtual reality and eye-tracking experimental study Meiqing Fu * , Rui Liu , Qipeng Liu M.E.

To address this issue, this study explores why individuals often fail to use emergency exit doors during evacuations via a virtual reality and eye-tracking experimental study and investigates human emergency wayfinding behaviors through the lens of perceptions and attention.
The results show that individuals ’ attention to wayfinding clues is positively related to their exit choices.
The experimental results reveal the conspicuity and visibility of exit doors and explicit and clear wayfinding information are crucial to increasing their usage during indoor evacuations.

This study focused on a typical wayfinding scenario, i.e., passing through a corridor with multiple exits, to examine the relationship be - tween individuals ’ visual attention and exit choice and explore why emergency exit doors are often underutilized in real evacuations. Particularly, this study focused on three factors, including familiarity, door color and type, and examined their effect on visual attention and exit choices. Familiarity, i.e., affiliative behavior, has been identified as one of the most important factors influencing exit choice [4,30]. The phenomenon that evacuees tend to evacuate by familiar exits has been widely observed in real evacuation [6], drills [7,31], field experiments [32], and VR experiments [33,34]. However, there is limited under - standing of why familiarity influences exit choices. This study aims to understand why familiarity affects individuals ’ wayfinding and exit choices during evacuations from the perspective of visual attention using eye-tracking techniques. Failure to notice an emergency exit door is a key contributor to explaining how familiarity affects the usage of the emergency exit door. Participants in the familiarity group were less likely to pay attention to the exit door and thus rarely use it. However, when participants had fixations on the door, their exit choices were not significantly different between the familiarity and unfamiliarity groups. In the present experiment, door color and type did not have a significant impact on participants ’ visual attention and exit choices. Specifically, the effect of door type on par - ticipants ’ exit choices was impaired by the presence of the stairwell sign. The experimental results reveal the conspicuity and visibility of exit doors and explicit and clear wayfinding information are crucial to increasing their usage during indoor evacuations. 1. Introduction Evacuation is a critical aspect of building safety. Proper evacuation procedures and protocols are essential to ensure the well-being of the occupants in case of fires, natural disasters, or other threats. These procedures typically include evacuation routes, exit signs, exit doors, emergency alarms, and many others. Exit doors are a crucial component of the egress system, and building codes accordingly specify detailed requirements for their number and dimensions. However, given the di - versity in building layouts, prescribing detailed criteria for the location of exit doors is impractical. Exit doors are required for separation dis - tance between exits and maximum exit access travel distance [1,2]. Typically, the access distance to exits is calculated based on the distance to the expected exit, which is often the nearest exit door. However, emergency exit doors may not be used as expected. Occupants do not always make optimal evacuation decisions [3]. They rarely escape via the nearest exit and tend to use familiar exits for evacuations [4,5]. In the survey of the Daegu subway fire, only 12 % of the survivors evac - uated using the designated routes and their nearest exits [6]. Rahouti et al. [7] executed an unannounced evacuation drill in a hospital setting. The findings revealed that both staff and patients predominantly chose to evacuate through entrances they were familiar with, rather than the nearest exits. evidenceSnippets.abstract: Abstract. With the increasing value generated by data curation and the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) agents that converse and act like human agents, vendor companies in established business-to-business (B2B) relationships increasingly delegate data curation tasks to algorithmic data requesters (ADRs) rather than human data requesters (HDRs). Firms employ these data requesters to email existing customers either to collect new infor - mation for improved services (data enrichment) or to update outdated information to maintain existing ones (data reconciliation). Despite the growing use of agents in data cura - tion, little is known about how customers respond to these practices—particularly how their responses vary by requester type (HDR versus ADR) and by the nature of the data work practice (enrichment versus reconciliation). Drawing on the effort-accuracy frame - work and gain-loss message framing, we investigate customer agreement with email- based data requests from HDRs (versus ADRs) in data enrichment (versus data reconcilia - tion) in a multimethod approach. Evidence from a randomized field experiment with a leading European pharmaceutical company followed by an online experiment reveals that customers have a reduced inclination to agree (versus disagree) with a data request from an HDR (versus ADR) in data enrichment because of their preference for minimizing effort in interactions with the data requester. However, for data reconciliation, customers prefer an HDR (versus ADR) because they have lower concerns about errors that could arise in these interactions. A post hoc analysis reveals that although the findings on customer agreement are supported for data enrichment (i.e., the customer completion rate is higher for ADRs versus HDRs), we find only marginal support for data reconciliation (i.e., the cus - tomer completion rate is only marginally higher for HDRs versus ADRs). Qualitative responses from a follow-up online survey and interviews with customers of the pharma - ceutical company corroborate and complement the main quantitative findings. Overall, this research expands our understanding of continued customer engagement in data cura - tion ...

Vendors that excel at eliciting positive customer responses to agent- based data curation practices tend to have more satis - fied customers and higher revenue than their market counterparts (e.g., Forrester 2024 , IBM 2024 ). However, more than half of companies currently fail to elicit such positive customer responses, resulting in missing or outdated customer data and consequently, subopti - mal customer value creation (e.g., Validity 2024 , Sales - force 2025 ). As improving customer responses to agent-based data curation practices benefits both ven - dors and customers, the phenomenon requires more theoretical and practical attention. Accordingly, the objective of this paper is to investigate customer responses to the emerging phenomenon of agent-based data curation practices . Notably, customer responses to agent-based data curation practices should not be seen as a one-time event. Instead, data curation practices unfold across the entire data life cycle, evolving alongside the busi - ness relationship—from initial data collection at the outset to ongoing data curation that supports retention and deeper engagement with customized services (e.g., Maass et al. 2018 , Mikalef et al. 2020 ). Ongoing data curation transforms customer data into a dynamic asset that enhances profile accuracy and depth— directly fueling customer retention and business growth. For instance, Netflix’s continuously enriched viewing data powers a recommender system responsi - ble for roughly 80% of streamed hours and saves over $1 billion annually through reduced churn (Gomez- Uribe and Hunt 2015 ). Similar patterns hold across industries; Gartner ( 2025 ) reports that poor data qual - ity costs firms at least $12.9 million per year, whereas companies excelling in data-enabled personalization— built on well-curated data—earn about 40% more reve - nue from these initiatives than competitors (McKinsey & Company 2021 ). evidenceSnippets.resultsDiscussion: results collected in a real event (8), and the outcomes obtained in highly competitive evacuation drills in which pedestrians were allowed to push each other (22). In these last two cases, very high densities were present (which dom- inate the dynamics) and the free velocities were below 1.5 m/s. Remarkably, the assumptions used for traditional fundamental diagrams are not valid in the Running of the Bulls Festival. Here, a moving threat (the bulls) induces time-dependent desired velocities along with a broad distribution among individuals. To understand the complicated dynamics observed, we characterize this system by studying—among other variables—the speed, den- sity, and falling probability of the pedestrians. The Pedestrian System During the week of the San Fermín festival, there is a bull run (“encierro”) every morning through the streets of Pamplona. The course is 875 m long, starting in a yard, and finishing in the bullring (see map in ref. 23). There, people run in front of six fighting bulls that are accompanied by six tamed bell oxen. Although the distance is not too long, it is impossible for a runner to cover the whole course for several reasons, such as the presence of other runners and, above all, the high speed of the bulls (the mean speed of the bulls, in our measurement areas, is 6 m/s). Significance A topic of special interest in crowd dynamics that can lead to better infrastructure management is the study of people under high competitiveness. Persons fleeing from real danger is one instance of this scenario, but of course it is difficult to analyze it experimentally. This is why people running with bulls at the San Fermín Festival provides an exceptional annual event where real data of pedestrian dynamics under extreme conditions can be collected. This kind of data is scarce and therefore highly valuable. qa.question: Why do you expect Signature2 to be highest?
qa.answer: Not because “medium information is inherently worse.” The mechanism is that Signature2 may provide enough information to require active interpretation but not enough redundancy to resolve uncertainty quickly. That should increase confirmation cost, scanning, dwell, and EEG load, especially at decision points.

qa.question: What if Signature2 is not highest?
qa.answer: Then the result still informs signage design. We would test whether load instead tracks information density, decision complexity, audio overlap, or map-specific difficulty. The hypothesis is a planned contrast, not a guaranteed result.

qa.question: What are the biggest threats to validity?
qa.answer: Unclear Signature manipulation, EEG movement artifacts, audio overlap with visual epochs, map-specific effects, trial order/familiarity, and interpreting behavior as cognitive load without EEG support. Each has a planned control or sensitivity analysis.

evidenceSnippets.abstract: abstractly rather than focusing on practical details necessary for successful way fi nding in that particular space. Another reason could be differences in processing related to different environmental scales. In the model town used in Hund et al. (2008), the environment was experienced via a survey perspective, perhaps rendering cardinal descriptions ef fi cient for way fi nding. Furthermore, the entire environment was visible throughout the task, which reduced memory demands relative to everyday way fi nding in large-scale environments that involve ground-level views in which only part of the route is visible at any given moment. Although this seems like a viable account for the model town, it does not explain why the indoor way fi nding task involving routes through a university building yielded similar results (Hund & Padgitt, 2010). A third explanation could be related to differences in the way fi nding tasks. For instance, Denis et al. (1999) gave participants a written version of the entire route to be followed and asked them to study it for 2 min. Participants then followed the route from memory. This is in contrast to Hund et al. (2008) and Hund and Padgitt (2010), where participants read each segment on note cards while navigating the routes. Different cognitive demands may emerge from these way- fi nding tasks, which may result in differences in ef fi ciency when following the descriptions. Although descriptive features, envi- ronmental space, and cognitive demands may all account for these discrepancies in way fi nding, individual differences in spatial skills also may play a role (Hegarty, Richardson, Montello, Lovelace, & Subbiah, 2002; Hund & Nazarczuk, 2009; Kato & Takeuchi, 2003). One important individual difference is sense of direction, or “ awareness of orientation or location ” (Kozlowski & Bryant, 1977, p. 178). Sense of direction is related to way fi nding such that people with a good sense of direction actively explore and attend to details in new environments, and they remember new routes better than do people with a poor sense of direction. evidenceSnippets.methods: Method 2.1. Participants Fifty-three college students (29 men, 24 women) participated. Their ages ranged from 19 to 31 years ( M ¼ 20.96 years). Data from two additional participants were omitted because of researcher error. Participants were recruited through the Department of Psychology college student participant pool and received credit in their psychology courses. 2.2. Apparatus and materials Descriptions. A set of four routes from starting locations to destinations was utilized. The starting locations and destinations were the windows overlooking the plaza and the computer class- room, the research classroom suite and the elevators, a laboratory and a classroom, and a classroom and an of fi ce, sampling every area of the basement of a university building. We created 7 descriptions of each route. The descriptions varied in their use of cardinal directions, distances, left-rights, and landmarks (either at choice or non-choice points, see Table 1 and Appendix), yielding 28 descriptions in total. Sense of direction. Sense of direction was measured using the Sense of Direction Scale, a self-report instrument that includes two questions utilizing a 5-point scale (Hund & Nazarczuk, 2009; Pazzaglia & DeBeni, 2001). Test-retest reliability averaged .93 when participants reported their sense of direction in sessions separated by 2 weeks e 3 months (Kozlowski & Bryant, 1977). Environmental familiarity and demographic information. Two items measured participants ’ familiarity with the campus building used in the study (Hund & Nazarczuk, 2009). These items probed overall familiarity and how often participants visited the fl oor during a typical week. 1 Participants also completed a brief demographic information form. 2.3. Design and procedure Participants were asked to rate each of the 28 way fi nding directions based on effectiveness using a 7-point scale, with 1 indicating a poor direction that does not allow one to easily reach the goal and 7 indicating an excellent direction that enables one to follow the directions and reach the goal without error or hesitation (Denis et al., 1999; Hund et al., 2008). qa.question: Why do you expect Signature2 to be highest?
qa.answer: Not because “medium information is inherently worse.” The mechanism is that Signature2 may provide enough information to require active interpretation but not enough redundancy to resolve uncertainty quickly. That should increase confirmation cost, scanning, dwell, and EEG load, especially at decision points.

qa.question: What if Signature2 is not highest?
qa.answer: Then the result still informs signage design. We would test whether load instead tracks information density, decision complexity, audio overlap, or map-specific difficulty. The hypothesis is a planned contrast, not a guaranteed result.

qa.question: How will you prove the Signature manipulation worked?
qa.answer: I will not rely on labels alone. I will build a signature_manipulation_table with information density, arrow count, exit count, redundancy, ambiguity, clarity, continuity, and decision relevance, plus post-trial ratings of clarity/reliability/overload and behavioral errors.

Another reason could be differences in processing related to different environmental scales. In the model town used in Hund et al. (2008), the environment was experienced via a survey perspective, perhaps rendering cardinal descriptions ef fi cient for way fi nding. Furthermore, the entire environment was visible throughout the task, which reduced memory demands relative to everyday way fi nding in large-scale environments that involve ground-level views in which only part of the route is visible at any given moment. Although this seems like a viable account for the model town, it does not explain why the indoor way fi nding task involving routes through a university building yielded similar results (Hund & Padgitt, 2010). A third explanation could be related to differences in the way fi nding tasks. For instance, Denis et al. (1999) gave participants a written version of the entire route to be followed and asked them to study it for 2 min. Participants then followed the route from memory. This is in contrast to Hund et al. (2008) and Hund and Padgitt (2010), where participants read each segment on note cards while navigating the routes. Different cognitive demands may emerge from these way- fi nding tasks, which may result in differences in ef fi ciency when following the descriptions. Although descriptive features, envi- ronmental space, and cognitive demands may all account for these discrepancies in way fi nding, individual differences in spatial skills also may play a role (Hegarty, Richardson, Montello, Lovelace, & Subbiah, 2002; Hund & Nazarczuk, 2009; Kato & Takeuchi, 2003). One important individual difference is sense of direction, or “ awareness of orientation or location ” (Kozlowski & Bryant, 1977, p. 178). Sense of direction is related to way fi nding such that people with a good sense of direction actively explore and attend to details in new environments, and they remember new routes better than do people with a poor sense of direction. evidenceSnippets.methods: Method 2.1. Participants Fifty-three college students (29 men, 24 women) participated. Their ages ranged from 19 to 31 years ( M ¼ 20.96 years). Data from two additional participants were omitted because of researcher error. Participants were recruited through the Department of Psychology college student participant pool and received credit in their psychology courses. 2.2. Apparatus and materials Descriptions. A set of four routes from starting locations to destinations was utilized. The starting locations and destinations were the windows overlooking the plaza and the computer class- room, the research classroom suite and the elevators, a laboratory and a classroom, and a classroom and an of fi ce, sampling every area of the basement of a university building. We created 7 descriptions of each route. The descriptions varied in their use of cardinal directions, distances, left-rights, and landmarks (either at choice or non-choice points, see Table 1 and Appendix), yielding 28 descriptions in total. Sense of direction. Sense of direction was measured using the Sense of Direction Scale, a self-report instrument that includes two questions utilizing a 5-point scale (Hund & Nazarczuk, 2009; Pazzaglia & DeBeni, 2001). Test-retest reliability averaged .93 when participants reported their sense of direction in sessions separated by 2 weeks e 3 months (Kozlowski & Bryant, 1977). Environmental familiarity and demographic information. Two items measured participants ’ familiarity with the campus building used in the study (Hund & Nazarczuk, 2009). These items probed overall familiarity and how often participants visited the fl oor during a typical week. 1 Participants also completed a brief demographic information form. 2.3.
